qti-choice-interaction.qti-prompt: As a hurricane neared, the county opened a public storm shelter and adopted a strict same-for-everyone rule: two buses to every neighborhood, no exceptions, even though the county's own transit survey showed which areas had almost no cars. Buses sat half-empty where most families could drive, while in the carless neighborhoods the two buses filled within minutes and hundreds of families were left to find their own way. Which description best fits the county's plan?
qti-choice-interaction.qti-simple-choice: Equitable, since giving every neighborhood an identical share of help is the very model of fairness.
Impartial, since the county treated every neighborhood exactly alike and favored none.
Lopsided, since the county piled its buses onto a single favored district.
Random, since the bus routes were assigned by chance with no rule behind them.

qti-content-body.p: Correct. The county played no favorites: two buses each, assigned by the same rule everywhere, with no district singled out for better or worse treatment. Refusing to favor any side is exactly what impartial means -- even when, as here, that evenhandedness ignores who actually needed the help.

Separate how the plan treated people from how well it worked. Every neighborhood got the same two buses under one published rule -- so nothing was lopsided and nothing was random. And a plan that leaves carless families stranded while buses sit half-empty has ignored people's differing needs, which real fairness to circumstances would have weighed. Which word names treating all sides exactly alike, favoring none?

Equitable fairness accounts for people's different needs and circumstances -- and the county had the needs in hand, since its own survey showed which areas had almost no cars. It sent those areas the same two buses anyway, leaving hundreds without a way out while other buses sat half-empty. Identical treatment that ignores known, unequal needs is evenhanded, but it is not equitable.

Lopsided would mean the help tilted heavily toward one favored side. No district got more than any other -- two buses each, everywhere, was the whole rule. The plan's flaw is that it refused to tilt even where the need was greatest, which is the opposite of lopsidedness.

Random would mean the routes came out of a hat, with no rule behind them. The rule here could not have been clearer: two buses to every neighborhood, no exceptions. A plan can follow a firm rule and still serve people poorly -- that does not make it chance.
